notes.meaning: God looks back to the early history of Israel when the people were helpless slaves in Egypt. Out of sheer fatherly love, He chose them, rescued them from slavery, and called them His own son. This shows that the nation's entire existence was founded on God's free grace and love.

differ.view: Some Baptist commentators hold that this verse refers primarily and directly to Jesus Christ rather than the nation of Israel, viewing the Exodus as only a picture of Christ coming out of Egypt.

notes.meaning: God sent prophet after prophet to urge Israel to return to Him, but the people turned a deaf ear and walked away. The more the prophets called, the more determined the people were to worship the local Canaanite idols known as the Baals. They repeatedly chose worthless statues over their living Father.

God describes Himself as a tender parent teaching a young child how to walk, holding Israel up by the arms so they would not fall. He guided and protected them all through their wilderness journey. Sadly, the people were completely blind to His loving care and never thanked Him for keeping them safe and healthy.

God led His people with gentle kindness and ropes of love, treating them like human beings rather than unmanageable beasts. He acted like a kind farmer who loosens the heavy wooden yoke from an ox's jaw so it can rest. Then God stooped down low to feed them bread from heaven in the desert.

Because the people stubbornly refused to repent and turn back to God, they would face exile and loss of freedom. They wanted to flee to Egypt for safety, but instead the brutal empire of Assyria would conquer them and become their new master. Refusing to return to God led straight into foreign captivity.

War would sweep through their towns like a flashing sword, tearing down the strong bars of their city gates. Their fortresses and mighty soldiers would not be able to defend them. Their own clever political schemes and alliances brought about their downfall instead of saving them.

God's people had a fixed habit of wandering away and sliding backward into sin. Even when God's messengers invited them to look up to the Most High God, hardly anyone was willing to honor Him. They clung to their idols instead of lifting their hearts to the Lord.

God reveals His deep, personal agony over handing His people over to punishment. Admah and Zeboiim were neighbouring cities destroyed alongside Sodom, but the Lord refuses to wipe out Israel completely like that. His fatherly pity and burning compassion surge forward, keeping His final wrath in check.

God promises that He will not wipe out Israel in hot fury, nor will He return to utterly destroy them. He explains that He is God and not a mortal man, so His mercy and covenant faithfulness far exceed human limits. Even in His righteous discipline, the Holy One among them will preserve a living remnant.

A future day will come when the scattered people will turn and follow the Lord. He will shout His royal summons like the loud roar of a lion, reaching across distant lands. Hearing His commanding voice, His children will hurry back to Him with reverent awe from the western islands and coasts.

The exiles will hasten back from Egypt and Assyria as swiftly as fluttering birds and doves returning to their nests. God promises to bring them home and settle them securely in their own houses once again. The Lord guarantees this restoration with His own dependable word.

The northern tribes of Israel constantly surrounded God with deceit and empty, hypocritical worship. In contrast, the southern kingdom of Judah still maintained true worship in the temple and remained loyal to the God of their holy ancestors. God sees through religious pretense, but He treasures genuine faithfulness.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern scholars translate this verse as a criticism of Judah as well as Israel, saying Judah was rebellious and unruly against the Holy One, and they place this line at the beginning of chapter 12.
